en: The Eight-Verse Hymn to Mahogratārā:
O Mother Nīlasarasvatī, bestower of good fortune and prosperity upon those who bow before you,
you who stand in the pratyālīḍha posture upon the heart of a corpse, with a smiling lotus-face!

O Goddess, you who possess three eyes like full-blown blue lotuses, and who hold a curved knife, a skull-cup, a lotus, and a sword—you alone are my refuge; I take shelter in you, the Sovereign Lady. || 1 ||

O Sovereign of Speech, O Wish-fulfilling Creeper for devotees, O Mistress of the accomplishment of all aims, O Bestower of the immediate attainment of every purpose in the composition of both prose and verse;
O You who possess three eyes like blue lotuses, O Ocean of Compassion!
Out of compassion, sprinkle those like us with the rain of the nectar of good fortune. || 2 ||
O you whose body is filled with the pride of dwarfishness, radiant with ornaments such as serpents,
beautiful with a tiger-skin girdle around your waist and marked by swinging bells,
[you who possess] the hair of two freshly severed heads shimmering with dust—
O terrifying one, beautiful with a garland of human heads and a string of knots, destroy my fear! || 3 ||
O You who consist of the forms of Māyā, Aṅga, Vikāra, Rūpa, Lalanā, Bindu, and Ardhacandra;

O You whose nature is the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*; O You whose essence is mantra—You alone are the refuge for one such as I. O Mother, Your form is threefold, fashioned from the three abodes: the gross, the extremely subtle, and the supreme.
For sensation is not within my range; how then could I possibly resort to it? || 4 ||
By serving your lotus feet, those of meritorious deeds attain union with that glorious Supreme Lord, whose nature is as gentle as the three-eyed Śiva and Brahmā;
[union] which even the gods, led by Indra, though their bodies are capable of sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra, do not attain.
O Mother, for what dull-witted person would serve one who is averse to serving Your feet? || 5 ||

O Mother, those gods and asuras who, bearing the seal of the pollen from the pair of your lotus feet upon their crowns, have entered your lap without fear as victors in the battle between gods and demons;
others, however, harbor the rivalry, "I am a god in this world, none is my equal."
Being equal to that [cause], these certainly go to destruction by themselves after such a long time.
By the mere remembrance of your name,
the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and yakṣas, as well as the lords of the nāgas,
the foremost of the daityas and dānavas, the sky-dwellers, and creatures such as tigers, become intent on flight and are unable even to look at you.
O Mother, the ḍākinīs and the wrathful destroyers have become men upon the surface of the earth for a moment. (7)

O Mother, by serving Your feet, those various powers indeed become perfected for men: the fortune of Lakṣmī, the hosts of Siddhas beginning with the Pādukāsiddhas, as well as the immobilization of waters on the field of battle, the paralyzing of elephant herds, and the power of enchantment.
One's beauty becomes exceedingly lovely and great, and even a fool becomes like Vācaspati. || 8 ||
The man who, being devoted, pure, and self-restrained, recites this beautiful eightfold hymn to Tārā in the morning, at midday, and in the evening; || 9 ||
One obtains divine poetic skill and becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures; having attained imperishable fortune and enjoyed pleasures as desired, || 10 ||
One shall attain fame, splendor, freedom from disease, and become beloved by all;
having achieved renown throughout the worlds, one shall finally attain liberation.
The Eight-Verse Hymn to the Illustrious and Fierce Tārā is complete.
